item.title: Southeast Asian leaders will call for peaceful resolutions of conflicts. Trump will join final talks
item.description:
Southeast Asian leaders will call for peaceful resolutions of conflicts. Trump will join final talks
Southeast Asian leaders will gather in the Philippine capital this weekend for the annual ASEAN summit that will focus on global conflictsByJIM GOMEZ Associated PressNovember 14, 2026, 1:11 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
MANILA, Philippines -- Some of the world’s most intractable conflicts will be high on the agenda when Southeast Asian leaders gather in the Philippine capital for annual summit meetings this weekend. U.S. President Donald Trump is expected to join them for the final talks.
The three-day summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and their Asian and Western counterparts starts Sunday in a heavily guarded convention center in Manila Bay.
According to drafts of prepared post-summit communiques seen by The Associated Press, no breakthroughs are expected in the discussions that will focus on calling for the peaceful resolution of the South China Sea disputes, the civil strife in Myanmar and the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine.
This year, the Philippines holds the rotating leadership of ASEAN, a conservative regional bloc of 11 democratic and authoritarian states, including police states. The bloc has managed to keep together such a diverse grouping since its founding in 1967 largely because of its bedrock policy of non-interference in the members' domestic affairs.
In Manila, key rivals will again be face-to-face but no shake-ups are anticipated. ASEAN is known more for its photo-ops that project unity, cultural pomp and pageantry than for effectively dealing with the region's conflicts, including the civil war in Myanmar.
Trump will land in Manila with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday afternoon, after the main ASEAN summit meetings have concluded and the Philippines has turned over the regional bloc’s annual leadership to Singapore.

item.title: Bomb rips through Damascus suburb killing 2 including a child
item.description:
Bomb rips through Damascus suburb killing 2 including a child
The device placed inside a car in a suburb of the Syrian capital.ByThe Associated PressNovember 14, 2026, 1:43 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
DAMASCUS, Syria -- An explosive device placed inside a car in a suburb of Syria's capital exploded Saturday evening, killing two people and wounding at least one, state TV and the Interior Ministry said.
The explosion took place in the southern Damascus suburb of Jaramana near a factory where batteries are produced, state TV said. It said two people were killed and two were wounded, without giving further details.
The Interior Ministry said the dead included a child, adding that one person was wounded. It said security forces cordoned off the area and started an investigation.

Several explosions have taken place in Damascus and its suburbs in recent months as the country’s security remains fragile nearly two years after five decades of Assad family rule ended in December 2024. Militants stormed the capital and removed then-President Bashar Assad from power.
Jaramana is home to a large community of the Druze religious minority. The suburb has faced tensions between some members of the community and Sunni Muslim Syrians supportive of the country’s current Islamist-led government.

item.title: Filipino singer Carmelle storms to victory in Eurovision Asia debut in Bangkok
item.description:
Filipino singer Carmelle storms to victory in Eurovision Asia debut in Bangkok
Filipino singer Carmelle won the first Asian edition of the Eurovision Song Contest with a fiery performance of “Sobra-Sobra,” beating 10 other acts in the grand final in BangkokByThe Associated PressNovember 14, 2026, 11:49 AM
Share
BANGKOK -- Filipino singer Carmelle won the first Asian edition of the Eurovision Song Contest on Saturday with a fiery performance of her dance-pop song “Sobra-Sobra.”
The 19-year-old beat 10 other acts in the grand final in Bangkok, with the winner chosen through votes from national juries in participating countries and viewers worldwide.
After her victory, Carmelle said her song celebrated female empowerment and was intended as “a tribute to all Filipino women.”
“I made history, since this was the first time,” she told The Associated Press. “It’s such a big responsibility for me, because this one is a global stage, so thank you everybody who voted for me.”
Thai duo Mang x Daou finished second with an energetic performance of the romantic pop song “Aroma.” Vietnam’s Tóc Tiên placed third with a lively, stylish rendition of “Em Tiên.”
Malaysia’s Aina Abdul took fourth with her powerful ballad “Bluest Sky.” Thinla of Laos finished fifth with “Bae,” a playful dance track that had the audience dancing whenever it was replayed during the show.
Bhutan, South Korea, Mongolia, Nepal, Cambodia and Bangladesh also competed.
Contestants made their entrances aboard tuk-tuks, the motorized three-wheeled vehicles common in Bangkok’s tourist districts. They waved national flags as thousands of fans cheered inside the city-center venue.
Bulgarian singer Dara appeared as a special guest, performing “Bangaranga,” the song with which she won the 70th Eurovision Song Contest in Vienna earlier this year.

item.title: Pope crosses Peru in finale of trip home to visit flock high in Andes, deep in Amazon
item.description:
Pope crosses Peru in finale of trip home to visit flock high in Andes, deep in Amazon
The plight of Indigenous peoples and the protection of the Amazon take center stage on Pope Leo XIV’s penultimate day in Peru as he visits communities in the Andes and the rainforestByMAURICIO SAVARESE Associated Press, NICOLE WINFIELD Associated Press, and ASTRID SUAREZ Associated PressNovember 15, 2026, 6:53 AM
Share
CUSCO, Peru -- The plight of Indigenous peoples and the protection of the Amazon take center stage Sunday as Pope Leo XIV travels across Peru to visit communities high in the Andes and deep in the rainforest.
On the penultimate day of his visit to his adopted homeland, Leo is expected to echo Pope Francis, emphasizing Catholic teaching that links care for the most vulnerable with care for God’s creation.
He travels first to Cusco, the former capital of the Inca empire, before flying to the Amazonian city of Pucallpa, where illegal mining, deforestation and threats to Indigenous communities will be central concerns.
“The church in Peru perceives the continuity of his commitment to accompany Indigenous peoples in the defense of life and the care of the territory, which is increasingly threatened by deforestation and illegal mining,” Peruvian Cardinal Pedro Barreto, president of the Amazon bishops conference, told The Associated Press.
“Leo is clearing the path laid out” by Francis on environmental protection and human rights, Barreto said. He added that the pope would hear about violence affecting children and young people.
The visit to Cusco, 3,400 meters (more than 11,000 feet) above sea level, will test the stamina of the pope, who is recovering from lung cancer surgery.
His schedule begins at the historic Sacsayhuamán fortress, where he will speak about local religious devotion. In the Plaza de Armas, he will present a shroud from the Holy See for the image of the Lord of the Earthquakes, a focus of devotion in a country prone to seismic activity. He will ...

item.title: Zelenskyy says a new European security framework floated by US could benefit Putin
item.description:
Zelenskyy says a new European security framework floated by US could benefit Putin
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says the U.S. has raised the idea of a new postwar security framework for EuropeByHANNA ARHIROVA Associated PressNovember 14, 2026, 6:21 AM
KYIV, Ukraine -- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the United States had raised the possibility of a new security framework for Europe as part of efforts to end Russia’s war in Ukraine, warning that Moscow could use such discussions to weaken NATO and reshape the continent’s borders.
Separately, Ukrainian forces struck a major Russian oil facility supporting Moscow’s war effort, Ukraine's General Staff said in a statement Saturday. Russian
“In my view, this can be dangerous,” Zelenskyy told reporters Friday, referring to the new security framework. “This should not be the main agenda.” His comments were embargoed until Saturday.
He said he believed Moscow was interested in reopening broader questions about European security rather than focusing exclusively on ending the 4 1/2-year war.
“(Russian President Vladimir) Putin’s desire to change borders in Europe is a fact. I am sure this is part of his concept of revising security guarantees in Europe,” he said. “This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations.”
European leaders have stressed that decisions about the continent’s security must be made by Europeans themselves, warning against allowing Russia to dictate the terms of a new security order or negotiate NATO's future.
Zelenskyy said the U.S. had asked for the first time whether Ukraine would withdraw from parts of the Donbas region in eastern Ukraine that Russia does not control if Kyiv were admitted to NATO. He reiterated that Kyiv would not surrender its territory.

item.title: Methane blast kills 2 at Colombian mine, search continues for 2 missing
item.description:
Methane blast kills 2 at Colombian mine, search continues for 2 missing
A methane explosion at a mine in central Colombia killed two workers and left two others missing, mining officials saidByThe Associated PressNovember 14, 2026, 12:54 PM
BOGOTA, Colombia -- Rescuers continued searching Saturday for two miners missing after an explosion killed two workers at a mine in rural central Colombia, officials said.
The National Mining Agency said on social media that rescuers were working at the mine, but a collapse caused by Friday’s methane gas explosion was hampering their efforts. Four miners were at the site when the blast occurred.
The mine is in Chita, a municipality in the department of Boyaca, about 149 miles (240 kilometers) north of Bogota. Boyaca Gov. Carlos Amaya said he was monitoring efforts to determine what caused the explosion.
Security camera footage broadcast by Colombian media showed a massive plume of black smoke and flames rising from the blast.

Mining accidents are common in central Colombia, where dozens of small-scale operators run coal and emerald mines.
The agency has previously warned that gases and dust can accumulate in coal deposits, creating hazardous conditions.

item.title: At least 6 killed and 11 injured when bus overturns in southwestern Colombia
item.description:
At least 6 killed and 11 injured when bus overturns in southwestern Colombia
Police report that at least six people are dead and 11 injured after a bus overturned on a highway in southwestern ColombiaByThe Associated PressNovember 14, 2026, 2:04 PM
BOGOTA, Colombia -- A bus overturned Saturday on a highway in southwestern Colombia, killing at least six people and injuring 11, the National Police said.
A police report seen by The Associated Press said the driver may have briefly fallen asleep at the wheel, causing the incident.
Videos shared on social media showed emergency personnel assisting injured passengers and people crying next to the overturned bus on the Garzon–Neiva highway. The bus, which was headed to the capital, Bogota, was later removed from the road and traffic was restored.
The police report states authorities were still trying to determine the exact circumstances under which the bus overturned in the department of Huila, but they believe the driver may have experienced an episode of “microsleep" — falling asleep for a few seconds.

item.title: South Sudan postpones first national elections again, to February 2027
item.description:
South Sudan postpones first national elections again, to February 2027
South Sudan has again postponed its first national elections since independence in 2011, moving polling from December to FebruaryByFLORENCE MIETTAUX Associated PressNovember 14, 2026, 5:57 AM
JUBA, South Sudan -- South Sudan has again postponed its first national elections since independence in 2011, moving polling from December to February amid concerns about insecurity, funding shortages and the country’s readiness to vote.
A revised timetable published Saturday by the National Election Commission sets Feb. 11, 2027, as polling day, replacing Dec. 22. The document did not give a reason for the postponement.
The polls have been repeatedly delayed, including in 2022 and 2024. The latest announcement follows warnings that elections could further unravel the country’s fragile peace.
The commission published the timetable on social media on the day voter registration was scheduled to begin. It also sets dates for candidate nominations and campaigning.
A day earlier, commission chairperson Gabriel Bol Deng told journalists in Juba that registration would run from Nov. 14 to Nov. 28 at 3,161 registration centers across the country’s 10 states and three administrative areas.
Deng urged eligible citizens to register and called on political parties, civil society groups, community leaders and the media to help raise public awareness.
South Sudan became independent from Sudan in 2011 after decades of civil war. A new conflict broke out in 2013 between forces loyal to President Salva Kiir and followers of his rival, Riek Machar. A peace deal was signed in 2018 and a transitional government of national unity was formed in 2020.

item.title: Pope laments violence enveloping Peru as he ministers in his former diocese
item.description:
Pope laments violence enveloping Peru as he ministers in his former diocese
Pope Leo XIV prayed for an end to the violence ravaging Peru, addressing one of his adopted homeland’s most pressing concerns from his former cathedralByNICOLE WINFIELD Associated Press, ASTRID SUAREZ Associated Press, and LUIS ANDRES HENAO Associated PressNovember 14, 2026, 11:14 AM
CHICLAYO, Peru -- CHICLAYO, Peru (AP) — Pope Leo XIV prayed Saturday for an end to the violence ravaging Peru, addressing one of his adopted homeland’s most pressing concerns during visits to his former cathedral and a remote community in his onetime diocese.
At Chiclayo’s cathedral, Leo entrusted his pontificate to the Virgin Mary in a special ceremony before traveling to Santa Cruz de Succhabamba, nestled in lush green mountains near the diocese’s outer reaches.
He traveled by helicopter to the city, 150 kilometers (93 miles) from central Chiclayo and 2,035 meters (6,675 feet) above sea level. The journey reflected his belief that shepherds must reach the peripheries to minister to their flocks.
Leo, formerly Robert Prevost, is beloved in the region for venturing beyond the sacristy to serve poor, outlying communities. As bishop, he would make the difficult drive to Santa Cruz de Succhabamba himself in his pickup truck.
“We all know the pope’s love of cars,” the Rev. Kevin Noriega, who oversees pastoral services, said before Mass. “He would drive everywhere.”
Before leaving, Leo led a special prayer at the Cathedral of St. Mary in Chiclayo, where he served as bishop from 2014 to 2023. He spoke of the “darkness” enveloping Peru, referring to rising crime amid political instability.
The homicide rate has nearly doubled over the past five years, from 5.8 to 10.7 per 100,000 people. Reports of extortion increased from 2,421 in 2019 to 26,734 in 2025, according to official data.

item.title: Cape Verde could elect first woman president since gaining independence in 1975
item.description:
Cape Verde could elect first woman president since gaining independence in 1975
Cape Verde could elect its first woman president as former Justice Minister Joana Rosa challenges incumbent José Maria NevesByThe Associated PressNovember 15, 2026, 12:22 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
Cape Verde could elect its first woman president Sunday as former Justice Minister Joana Rosa challenges incumbent José Maria Neves, who is seeking a second term.
Six candidates are competing, with a runoff scheduled for Nov. 29 if no candidate receives more than half the votes.
Rosa, backed by the opposition Movement for Democracy, is the first woman to run for president since independence from Portugal in 1975. Women have held senior cabinet posts, but Cape Verde has never had a female prime minister or president.
In Cape Verde’s parliamentary system, the prime minister directs government policy and holds most executive authority. The president’s role is largely symbolic, although the directly elected head of state can veto legislation.
The Atlantic island nation off West Africa, home to about half a million people, has a record of peaceful transfers of power and competitive elections in a region where that is rare. Nearly 77,000 Cape Verdeans abroad are registered to vote, almost a fifth of the total electorate.
Many voters feel distant from their leaders and want a president who understands their daily difficulties, while limited economic prospects were driving young people to seek opportunities abroad, said Roselma Évora, a professor of political science and gender studies at the University of Cabo Verde.
Neves, who won in 2021 with about 52% of the vote, has pledged to build cross-party support to improve housing, healthcare and education, create jobs and raise wages.
Incumbency gives Neves greater visibility, including among overseas voters, Évora said.
